newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal PM threatens resignation, bill defeated.
newsitem.headline: Portugal PM threatens resignation, bill defeated.

text.p: Prime Minister Antonio Guterres said on Thursday his government would quit if parliament pushed through a bill on local government spending that would harm Portugal's chances of joining the European single currency.
Earlier, opposition parties rejected a government bill on local government financing. In a parliamentary vote, opposition parties cast 109 votes to reject the bill against 102 in favour.

"If a local financing bill receives final approval that leads to an increase in taxes and an aggravation of the public deficit, I shall no longer have the conditions to govern," Guterres said in an address to the nation broadcast on live television.

"The final approval by parliament of a bill that goes against our electoral promises, sacrificing the Portuguese to a brutal increase in taxes or an aggravation of the deficit, that would derail us from the path we have been taking in Europe, will lead immediately to my offer to resign," he added.
"I hope that this does not happen, as no one will oblige me or the government to govern against our own programme voted for by the Portuguese," the Socialist prime minister said.
"Today I will take no decision that will create a political crisis, a crisis that I do not want and that the Portuguese certainly do not want," he added.

Guterres's government has said that opposition proposals for local government financing, which increase the funding received by local authorities, would boost overall public expenditure and lead to tax rises.

In May, parliament approved the general text of the opposition proposals, the first step towards their eventual adoption by the legislature. Parliament is due to reach a final decision on the proposals in September.
The government's unsuccessful bill proposed granting increased powers to local authorities, but did not increase their funding.

Guterres's government was elected in October 1995 after pledging to lead Portugal into the European single currency from the start in 1999 and promising not to raise taxes, but its victory fell four seats short of an absolute majority.

Guterres said in May that he wanted early elections if the main opposition parties received parliamentary approval for local government spending plans that would lead to tax rises and jeopardise Portugal's entry to the single currency, or euro.
Any decision to call early elections would be taken by President Jorge Sampaio.
